issues.title: Interworking with Other Congestion Management Mechanisms
issues.author: anooptomar29
issues.body: SCONE most often gets confused with transport level congestion control mechanism such as L4S/ECN-EC. So it will help to explicitly clarify here that SCONE is not meant for transient congestion control  (due to varying load and/or varying channel conditions) of the bottleneck link (such as air interface or any other bottleneck link).  Both the mechanisms i.e SCONE and L4S are intended to address different scenario/use-case in the network. And if needed, both can co-exist in the network as they complement each other.

issues.title: In Section 3.5: How is retransmission realized?
issues.author: gorryfair
issues.body:
The current text says:
  "Both SCONE Network Elements and application endpoints should support retransmission or periodic re-sending of SCONE packets to ensure reliable delivery."

- Please say more about how a network element perform retransmission of the SCONE Packets? What specifically is retransmitted and how?

comments.body: This section needs to be removed as it does not comply with the protocol spec

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
> "Both SCONE Network Elements and application endpoints should support retransmission or periodic re-sending of SCONE
packets to ensure reliable delivery."

> Please say more about how a network element perform retransmission of the SCONE Packets? What specifically is retransmitted and how?

We addressed this specific point in PR29. The PR covers the point that  a Network Element cannot perform transport-layer retransmissions because it cannot synthesize or inject new SCONE packets. Instead, it relies on the application endpoints to send the packets periodically. There are additional comments from Mirja and Marcus that have to be considered so final text will likely be tweaked.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
@gorryfair 
Recapping here once to more so we can drive towards closing the issue.

Reworked in PR #29. The section (now "Reliability and Mitigating Packet Loss") clarifies that a network element does not perform transport-layer retransmission and cannot inject SCONE packets. Reliable delivery relies on application endpoints sending SCONE packets periodically, with the network element updating traversing packets at an operationally chosen frequency.

issues.title: In Section 3.3: Please consider the interaction with other configured IP mechanisms.
issues.author: gorryfair
issues.body:
Ought there to be some consideration of how a Scone signal interacts with diffserv and other methods?

- What is intended to happen when an application uses two (or more) DSCPs? (Section 5.3 of the protocol spec alludes to this, but I expected some explanation in the applicability-manageability draft?

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
@gorryfair Thanks for raising this. To point you to where the document already speaks to IP-layer interaction: the Interworking with Other Congestion Management Mechanisms section notes that SCONE advice is carried within the QUIC payload and is independent of the IP-layer ECN field, so it neither reads nor modifies IP-layer markings.

What we cover: that independence, framed around ECN and L4S. The same reasoning extends to DiffServ and DSCP, since SCONE keys on the UDP 4-tuple and operates in the QUIC payload, so it does not depend on or interact with DSCP marking. On the case you raised of an application using more than one DSCP, because the advice is associated with the 4-tuple rather than the marking, multiple DSCPs on the same flow do not change which flow the advice applies to.

What we do not cover: we do not currently call out DiffServ or DSCP by name, since we have treated it as part of the general IP-layer independence above rather than as a separate mechanism.

Would the current treatment in the Interworking section be acceptable to you, or would you prefer we add an explicit sentence generalizing the independence from ECN to IP-layer markings including DSCP? If we do not hear a preference by Friday, June 12, we will close this on the basis that the independence is already covered, and we can revisit if needed.

comments.author: gorryfair
comments.body: This new text appears clear. I suspect a network might reserve/prioritise resources based on a DSCP, but in this framing I think that would be one input to the Network Element to figure out the guidance. I am not sure of the wisdom of explaining this outside of a concrete example. I think we could close this particular issue.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body: Closing per Gorry's confirmation. The new text is clear, and the DSCP interaction is best left to a concrete example rather than described in the abstract.

issues.title: Discuss network deployment use cases with or without throttling fallback
issues.author: mirjak

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: Specifically section 3.9 should talk more about how to do compliance measurements, e.g. using a sliding window, and what to do if a violation is detected

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body: Thank you for this feedback. Agree that we need to clarify how measurements are done and what the fallback options are when a violation is detected. We can rewrite Section 3.9 (Conformance Monitoring) to explicitly describe using a sliding window approach (evaluating flows against the highest limit advised over the preceding two monitoring periods) to account for application adaptation time. And also add explicit guidance on operator deployment choices when a violation is detected, for example, operators can either employ a throttling fallback (falling back to traditional rate-limiting mechanisms like dropping or delaying packets) or choose a purely advisory deployment without strict enforcement.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
@mirjak 
Following up on my April 26 note, both pieces are now in the Conformance Monitoring section, merged via PR #33:
- Sliding-window measurement: "Operators can accommodate this by utilizing a sliding window approach… evaluate QUIC flows against the highest throughput limit advised over the preceding two monitoring periods (a span of 134 seconds)…"
- Deployment choice on a detected violation: "…the network can employ a throttling fallback… such as dropping or delaying packets… Alternatively, operators can deploy SCONE purely as an advisory signal without any throttling fallback, prioritizing cooperative application optimization over strict compliance enforcement."
 
I believe this covers the with/without-throttling-fallback deployment discussion you raised. I plan to close the issue Friday, June 12, please let me know before then if you prefer to keep it open?

issues.title: Explain scone in masque proxies
issues.author: mirjak
issues.body: A masque proxy could also serve as scone network element. Would be good to have a short section to describe that this is possible if scone advice is applied before/after en/de-capsulation. Also there might also be a case to use scone for tunnel traffic...? If that's a case maybe we need to discuss how to copy over the outer scone to the inner scone?

comments.author: zaheduzzaman
comments.body:
Yes, a masque proxy , infact any proxy can be a network element that provides throughput advice. If we start treating masque proxy just more than an network element , then I think it gets a bit complicated. 

I think you are asking -

1) what happens when a masque proxy receives a SCONE packet, in that it would like to convey the throughput advice.
2) what happens when a masque proxy seceives a SCONE packet which already have a thgouthput advice.

in both cases the receiver is the same application that the SCONE packet is traveling to. Hence, it does not really matter if for case 1) if the masque proxy inserts the throughput advice in the tunneled packetd on non-tunnled packet. 

However, For 2) it might matter if the masque proxy passes through the throughput advice in the tunneled traffic and provides a different value in the outter QUIC. In that case, the applicaiton receiving two different values should gracefully handle the situation by taking the minimum of the throughput values as a described in the SCONE protocol specification.  We can remind readers on that. 

And perhaps ask not to send scone advice in both tunnelled and otter QUIC connection but we are not allowing the network element to create a SCONE packet of their own, so  to me this case does not exists.

This is covered in PR #33 which states, When evaluating compliance, network operators will need to account for the time required for SCONE packets to be updated, received by endpoints, and acted upon by the application. Specifically, as established in {{Dynamic Updates}} section, operators should evaluate QUIC flows against the highest throughput limit advised over the preceding two monitoring periods (a span of 134 seconds). If a network element cannot update the throughput advice in every traversing SCONE packet, operators might configure a longer sliding window to account for the possibility of packet loss.
To simplify the measurement function, reduce computational load, or offload this function to another node in the network, operators can select any value larger than the baseline 67-second window for their measurement and averaging period.

issues.title: Specification of retransmission belongs in main spec, not management
issues.author: huitema
issues.body:
The section on "Retransmission of Advised Bit-Rate" is written as advice to both Network Elements and application endpoints:

_Packet loss or non-delivery of SCONE advice reduces its effectiveness. Both SCONE Network Elements and application endpoints should support retransmission or periodic re-sending of SCONE packets to ensure reliable delivery. Conformance depends on the behavior of both network and application endpoint._

I wonder whether we need this section at all. The application endpoints behavior is defined in the protocol specification, and does not have a concept of "retransmission". Reliability is affected by two decisions:

1. The client should send scone packets with sufficient frequency,
2. The network elements should process a sufficient number of these packets.

This is specified in section "8.1.  Providing Opportunities to Apply Throughput Advice Signals" of the main spec. I really wonder whether we need to paraphrase that text here.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
@huitema, I have a following pending PR that has revised the text including the heading. You can see PR #29. It fully removes the text which you raised above. 

For ease, I am pasting the proposed text of PR here. 

**Mitigating Packet Loss:**
Packet loss or non-delivery of SCONE advice directly reduces its effectiveness. Because the reliable delivery of throughput advice relies entirely on the periodic sending of SCONE packets by application endpoints, the network element needs to make independent operational decisions on how frequently to update those traversing packets. This decision relies on operational considerations such as CPU load and the nature of the network policies. 

A network enforcing dynamic policies might prioritize updating SCONE packets immediately upon a policy trigger to minimize the application's reaction time to the new limit. Conversely, a network enforcing fixed, subscription-based policies can safely scale back its update frequency to conserve CPU resources, provided it still updates SCONE packets periodically (e.g., every 20 to 30 seconds). This periodic update frequency ensures that the throughput advice reliably reaches the endpoint and does not inadvertently expire across the standard monitoring period due to normal packet loss.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body: Closing. The retransmission text flagged here was reworked in PR #29 into the Reliability and Mitigating Packet Loss section, which @huitema reviewed and approved on May 9. Endpoint behavior now references Section 7.1 of the SCONE protocol rather than restating it, and only the operational update-frequency guidance remains in this document.

issues.title: Network elements dealing with overload
issues.author: huitema
issues.body:
The spec says that for a given flow (4 tuple), network elements should update at least one SCONE packet every 20-30 seconds. That's fine, but it creates a base load proportional to the number of 4 tuples seen by the network element. Potentially, there could be 2**(number of local addresses bits + number of remote addresses bits + 16 bits of local ports + 16 bits of remote ports) flows. There will generally be much less flows than that, but very large numbers could be seen, for example, during a DOS attack.

At that point, there are two plausible mitigations: either design the network element in such a way that it can update scone packets at line rate; or, fail gracefully. We may want to provide guidance on what "failing gracefully" means. The opposite of gracefully would be updating some of the flows some of the time in a random process, resulting in many flows receiving inconsistent advice, such as updates spaced by much more than 67 seconds. The clients would then be alternating between SCONE and non-SCONE mode, which seems bad.

Should that be discussed in the operational considerations?

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
@huitema agreed this is worth covering, and it could sit in the Appman document. Some early thinking before any text.

The per-flow refresh obligation makes SCONE load scale with the number of concurrent flows, which can spike well beyond normal during a flood or DoS. There can be two options here: provision the network element to refresh at line rate for the expected peak, or fail gracefully past that point.

For graceful degradation, one idea might be to shed whole flows rather than do partial random updates, so a flow gets either reliable in-cadence advice or none at all, and not intermittent advice that lapses past the 67-second window and makes the client flap between SCONE and non-SCONE. Which flows are served could follow operator policy and change with hysteresis to avoid churn, with shed flows falling back to normal forwarding.

Given that SCONE is now a work item in 3GPP, though I'm not yet sure what scope it will take there. Assuming some of these aspects end up being defined in 3GPP, it still seems worth identifying the conditions and noting possible mitigations in this document, as a guide. The network element vendor would expose the knobs and the operator tunes them, but the awareness of when overload arises and how to control it belongs here.

Does this capture your intent, and does this level of detail feel right. And yes,  operational considerations might be the place where this can be added.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
This PR #56  adds a new section, "Network Element Overload Handling," to address issue #41 raised by @huitema.

The section is placed after "Considerations of Processing Complexity," which establishes that SCONE reduces network
element CPU burden in the normal operating case. The new section addresses the edge case where that burden is exceeded
due to an unusually high number of concurrent SCONE flows, as can occur during periods of elevated traffic or network
stress.

Section 3.9:

You list useful logging topics and Section 3.10 covers conformance, but neither
section gives an operator a way to confirm the full loop, that advice was

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
Hi @mirjak thanks for the feedback.

Quick clarification first: I assume 'migration' in your comment was a typo for 'mitigation,' since the section focuses on mitigating packet loss (QUIC connection migration is discussed later). Let me know if I misunderstood that.

**Regarding the title:** I would prefer to keep 'Mitigating Packet Loss'. The section explicitly opens by noting that 'packet loss or non-delivery of SCONE advice directly reduces its effectiveness,' and the subsequent text directly notes that operators may update packets more frequently 'to better mitigate packet losses'. The focus is deliberately on mitigation, rather than being leftover text from an earlier draft.

**Regarding the overlap with Frequency of Updates:** I think the two sections are addressing fundamentally different mechanisms, even though both touch on 'frequency.'

**Frequency of Updates (Section 3.6) acts as the ceiling:** It defines how often SCONE packets exist for the network element to act upon at all, which is an endpoint-driven constraint entirely outside the network's control.

**Reliability and Mitigating Packet Loss (Section 3.5) acts as the floor:** Given that available ceiling, it dictates how aggressively the network element chooses to process and rewrite advice during the opportunities it does get. This is a network-side policy decision, bounded below by the 20 to 30 second baseline.

Because one is an endpoint constraint and the other is a network policy choice, I do not think merging them would help here. However, I agree that we should resolve the feeling of duplication. I propose adding a clarifying sentence to the beginning of Section 3.5 to make this 'ceiling versus floor' distinction explicit.

Proposed addition to Section 3.6 Frequency of Updates: [Add this as the starting sentence]
While the network element determines how often to update available SCONE packets to mitigate loss (as described in {{section-3.4}}), the absolute frequency of traversing SCONE packets is fundamentally bounded by the application endpoint's signaling cadence.
 
What do you think of this proposed addition? Would it help clarify the distinction for readers? I can propose this as suggestion to section.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body:
I think these are closely related. That the scone packet frequency is determined they the endpoint is a given and not part of the guidance provided; it's background information to understand the guidance on how the network operators apply its own frequency. Similar that packet loss will impact that frequency is still something that needs to be understood to understand the provided guidance of 20 to 30 secs. The import part is really to make the operators guidance clear and crisp. 

I created a PR (see #62) which makes this more clear as it takes all together: as such I also merged the section on "dynamic updates" in (as there was quite some redundancy). Also I would move the section on "[Network Element Overload Handling](https://ietf-wg-scone.github.io/appman/draft-ietf-scone-applicability-manageability.html#name-network-element-overload-ha)" then after this section.

issues.title: Policies to determine throughput advice
issues.author: mirjak
issues.body:
The section on "Determining Throughput Constraints" has the following bullet points:

>Application-Specific Policies: Operators may set maximum bit-rates for certain types of traffic based on subscription tier or device type, for example video optimization for adaptive bitrate video, or traffic shaping for low-priority bulk transfers such as background software updates.[¶](https://ietf-wg-scone.github.io/appman/draft-ietf-scone-applicability-manageability.html#section-3.2-2.2.1)

>Dynamic Network Conditions: Constraints may be updated as network conditions change, for example when a flow moves to a different access network.[¶](https://ietf-wg-scone.github.io/appman/draft-ietf-scone-applicability-manageability.html#section-3.2-2.3.1)

>Capacity and Load Management: During periods of unusually high usage, sustained overuse, or temporary equipment faults, the network element may temporarily lower its throughput advice to manage shared capacity and guide application usage.[¶](https://ietf-wg-scone.github.io/appman/draft-ietf-scone-applicability-manageability.html#section-3.2-2.4.1)

Part of the idea of scone is actually that you don't have to play an application-specific policies. The idea is really that instead of DPI you apply the advice to all flows that indicate SCONE support. Therefore I would prefer to remove that bullet or even state that this is not recommended.

On the other two (dynamic network conditions and Capacity/Load), aren't these the same? Usually you don't change the advice only because you change cell, it rather than the new cells as a different capacity/load profile and there also has a different advice. Maybe we can remove the bullet point on dynamic network conditions and add a sentence that capacity/load might change because of network changes such as moving to a different call. Btw. changing the entire access network is not a valid example here because that would mean the network element would change as well; so there are two different independent policies applied by two different operators; this is already further discussed in the section on [Presence of SCONE Network Elements On the Data Path](https://ietf-wg-scone.github.io/appman/draft-ietf-scone-applicability-manageability.html#name-presence-of-scone-network-e).

Also I recommend adapting a title a bit. I don't think "constraints" is a right word. Maybe the word "policy" should show up instead? Like "Applying network policies to determine throughput advice"?

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: Also not that (access) network changes are already covered in the section on "Changes of network element"; of course if you move to a different network/scone element that element might apply a different policy but that is not a change in policy.

issues.title: Expand Conformance Measurement section: explain sources of monitoring-window delay + tighter-window example
issues.author: smishra1200
issues.body:
Edit (2026-09-29): updated to reflect the discussion on #112. Loss, not packet-gap cadence, is the dominant factor.

draft-ietf-scone-protocol's Section 7.2 (Monitoring Flows) says the recommended monitoring window spans two monitoring periods to compensate for additional delays as SCONE packets are not delivered reliably, with other delays considered negligible by comparison (added via PR #159).

This issue proposes expanding Appman's Conformance Measurement section with the fuller version of that reasoning, following up on Martin Thomson's explanation on the list (responding to Gorry Fairhurst's AD review, 2026-08-11):

- unpacking what that margin covers (packet loss is the dominant factor, since each lost update delays the advice until the network element's next update, while network and endpoint processing delay is negligible)
- when a network element might justify a shorter monitoring window (e.g. restarting the monitoring period once it has updated at least two SCONE packets with the new advice, so a single lost update does not delay the advice)
- the tradeoff that stricter-than-baseline monitoring risks misclassifying a compliant application as non-conformant, per the protocol's own caution in Section 7.2

issues.title: Gorry's -03 review: tunnels and encapsulation (Section 3.13)
issues.author: smishra1200
issues.body:
From Gorry Fairhurst's review of -03 on the SCONE list:
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/scone/Zhk2YutZbsiSCAzHtiu3BS77vto/

> Section 3.13+ Missing mention of simple tunnels
>
> - I still think that there really ought to be a short section on "tunnels and encapsulation" in general. Encapsulating protocols is common, as is the use of tunnels for traffic engineering, VPN, etc. I'd love to see a very short section that calls out that using a tunnel/encaps can result in making it harder (or impossible) for the network element to locate a SCONE Packet, and if it fails to observe the packet, then the flow will not receive SCONE throughput advice.

> Section 3.13
>
> I have various comments on this section and a plea for a better structure.
>
> - So, when the SCONE packet is tunnelled over SCONE we have an important use case. MASQUE is a concrete example of this, but not the only possibility, and although we really ought to have text on MASQUE, most of this text is not specifically MASQUE, it is about a QUIC in QUIC tunnel. Could we clarify that please?
>
> - I do not understand the words  /fully encapsulated/ - could this be explained?
>
> - I expect the current text covers aggregation of multiple SCONE flows within a single QUIC flow in more than one para in this section - and really I think it would be much clearer if the section first said what happens if there is a single SCONE flow within the tunnel, and how the advice could be updated when the tunnel egress is a SCONE Network Element.
>
> - Separately we I wonder if the draft can then say  what is the implication if there is additional traffic in the tunnel and the tunnel enables SCONE, this is OK, but if there is a policy to control use of SCONE, this could result in the aggregate exceeding the throughput advice.
>
> - Then finally, I'd love to see text that gathers the advice on how to treat aggregates of more than one SCONE flow. Again, this might (or might not) result in a compliant SCONE tunnel. When the tunnel egress is a SCONE Network Element, I thin k we ought to apply advice on the multiple inner SCONE flows, and to say what are the expectations for policing.
>
> - I don't think the approach is a problem - but I am worried that too many variations  in operation could result in paths that are difficult to test!

comments.body: I think discussion is still on-going here, no?

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
@mirjak, Updated text and heading.  Please see if this addresses issues?


Major updates include:
1. Removed the phrase "the network element must make independent operational decisions". Softened it to "needs to make independent operational decisions" to ensure we aren't creating new pseudo-requirements outside of the core protocol document.
2. Changed the title from "Retransmission of Rate of Advised Bit-rates" to "Mitigating Packet Loss".

Please see the revised text:

**Mitigating Packet Loss:**
Packet loss or non-delivery of SCONE advice directly reduces its effectiveness. Because the reliable delivery of throughput advice relies entirely on the periodic sending of SCONE packets by application endpoints, the network element needs to make independent operational decisions on how frequently to update those traversing packets. This decision relies on operational considerations such as CPU load and the nature of the network policies. 

A network enforcing dynamic policies might prioritize updating SCONE packets immediately upon a policy trigger to minimize the application's reaction time to the new limit. Conversely, a network enforcing fixed, subscription-based policies can safely scale back its update frequency to conserve CPU resources, provided it still updates SCONE packets periodically (e.g., every 20 to 30 seconds). This periodic update frequency ensures that the throughput advice reliably reaches the endpoint and does not inadvertently expire across the standard monitoring period due to normal packet loss.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body: submitted and merged the PR per discussions.

This is pretty much right, but the endpoints can not take element CPU into consideration. 
Endpoints can send as frequently as they see fit, but the elements make decisions on update frequency based on considerations of CPU-load etc.

There is an additional consideration here. 
A network that has dynamic policies will likely care much more about timely updates than a network that has fixed policies (e.g., subscription-based policies that are not intended to change over SCONE-like timescales).
This paragraph should be removed as it is redundant to the spec and it's not good to say the same thing twice with different words.
Where does this number come from? This should not provide different/contradicting advice to the main spec.

Agree that Applicability document should guide operators rather than rehash core protocol mechanics. The above two paragraphs can be removed entirely so we are not repeating the endpoint sending behaviors already defined in Sections 7.1 and 8.1 of the main spec.

You are right to point this out and I agree. Endpoints have no visibility into a Network Element's CPU load and will send packets at their own pace. i can rewrite this paragraph to clarify that balancing CPU load and update frequency is strictly an operational configuration choice made by the network element, independently of the endpoint.

The 20 to 30 second value was actually drawn directly from Sections 7.1 and 8.1 of the core SCONE protocol specification, which state that updating every 20 to 30 seconds is likely sufficient. However, because per your above comments, I will be removing the redundant protocol explanations including removing these numbers entirely to avoid any perceived contradiction with the main spec.

This is an excellent operational consideration and exactly the kind of deployment guidance this document needs. I can incorporate this distinction into the text to highlight that dynamic policies require timely updates, whereas fixed subscription policies allow operators to scale back the update frequency to save CPU resources.

Could we add a reference to the Scone Transport spec, section 7.1.  Applying Throughput Advice Signals?

I think that what we are addressing here are an area voluntarily left unspecified by the specification, because of the tension between reliability and CPU load. The transport specification acknowledges that the network elements might not process every SCONE packet, and only mandate that "Senders that send a SCONE packet or network elements that update SCONE packets every 20–30 seconds is likely sufficient to ensure that throughput advice is not lost."

A conforming network element will process at least one packet every "20 to 30 second", but may want to process them more often, either to better mitigate packet losses or to ensure timely notifications. The appman document could say that and provide guidance.

Also, the title of this section should not be just about packet loss. It is about reliability, load and update frequency.

Hi Christian, Yes, I can definitely add the reference to the  Section 7.1 "Applying Throughput Advice Signals" and retune the text. 

RE the title change, I will note that we have a separate sub-section on Frequency of Updates and also a sub-section on Considerations of Processing Complexity that discusses load, so want to avoid, using frequency & load in the title, but, how about " Reliability & Mitigating Packet Loss"? 

I can update with a new PR with above changes including some tweaking of the text? Sound good?

@huitema, here is the proposed text and I can submit this on top of the last PR subject to feedback. Here is the text:

**3.4. Reliability and Mitigating Packet Loss**
Packet loss or non-delivery of SCONE advice directly reduces its effectiveness. Because the reliable delivery of throughput advice relies entirely on the periodic sending of SCONE packets by application endpoints, Section 7.1 ("Applying Throughput Advice Signals") of {{I-D.ietf-scone-protocol}} leaves the exact update frequency flexible. This flexibility allows operators to manage the tension between signaling reliability and network CPU load.

Ideally, a network element updates advice in SCONE packets at least twice per the 67-second monitoring period (approximately every 20 to 30 seconds), but operators may choose to process and update SCONE packets more frequently to better mitigate packet losses or to ensure timely notifications to the application. Therefore, the network element needs to make independent operational decisions on how frequently to update those traversing packets. A network enforcing dynamic policies might prioritize updating SCONE packets immediately upon a policy trigger to minimize the application's reaction time to the new limit. Conversely, a network enforcing fixed, subscription-based policies can safely scale back its update frequency to the 20 to 30-second baseline to conserve CPU resources. This baseline periodic update frequency ensures that the throughput advice reliably reaches the endpoint and does not inadvertently expire across the standard 67-second monitoring period due to normal packet loss.

Operators balancing this reliability against network element overhead can refer to the sections on Frequency of Updates and Considerations of Processing Complexity for further guidance.

Looks good, except for the word "Ideally". This is not an abstract ideal, it is the spec. Saying something like "A network element updates advice in SCONE packets at least twice per the 67-second monitoring period.." would be less ambiguous. Also, this is twice for each 4-tuple, but I guess this is discussed elsewhere.

@huitema,  I have removed "Ideally" to make the baseline expectation unambiguous. The sentence now says, "A SCONE-enabled network element updates advice in SCONE packets at least twice per the 67-second monitoring period (approximately every 20 to 30 seconds),....". And, yes,  the 4-tuple is covered explicitly in Flow Awareness and Per-Flow Signaling, which notes that throughput advice is applied on a UDP 4-tuple basis, so we don't need to repeat it in this section. 

I have submitted the revised PR.

comments.author: billwuqin
comments.body:
How this section is related to section 5.4 Following Throughput Advice and section 6.3 on Indications for Migrated Flows in SCONE base protocol? 
Be careful the boundary with SCONE protocol.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
@billwuqin,

Thank you. Good point on the boundary pointing to Sections 5.4 and 6.3 of the Protocol Spec. As these are both endpoint behavior in the protocol, i.e., Sec 5.4 is how an application follows advice, and 6.3 is how an endpoint re-indicates support on a new path after migration. The Dynamic Updates section is network-element-side and does not restate either.

Its basis is Section 9.2 of the protocol, which permits a network element to update more often immediately after a change in its throughput advice, to reduce the sender's reaction time. The section gives operators the deployment guidance to do that. That is, write the new value into the next traversing SCONE packet rather than wait for the periodic cadence.

That said, Improvements were definitely needed and I'm glad you raised the questions. The new edits dropped the access-network-handover example since a move to a different network element is the migration case covered by Section 6.3 and the Change of Network Element section in PR #32. I have now added a cross-reference to Section 9.2 to anchor this guidance in the protocol.

I don't understand what is meant by "opportunistically update the very next available SCONE packet(s) rather than waiting for its normal interval". Can you explain further?

Section [9.2 ](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-scone-protocol-04#name-damage-to-other-protocols)of SCONE Protocol explicitly states: "Network elements MAY update more often immediately after a change in their throughput advice, to reduce the reaction time from senders." 

Building on this, the PR uses the phrase "opportunistically update" to clarify that following a dynamic network change, a Network Element does not need to wait for the full 67-second monitoring period to elapse. Instead, it takes immediate advantage of the very next available endpoint-generated packet to deliver the updated throughput advice, minimizing the application's reaction time.

of course it doesn't. Why would it not add a new value to the available scone packet and then, of course, re-start the monitoring at the same time or actually wait one monitoring period from that point on. I find this text confusing...

The PR is trying to say, if there are events such as change in network or subscription policy, network does not have to wait for the full 67-second window to update ( ie add a new value in SCONE packet). Network element can "time" such updates to coincide with the "change" in policy (whatever that may be). RE re-starting monitoring, I assume you mean, reset the 67-second timer. I think, this is a very good suggestion. Happy to add that text, but, if we want this as a requirement, then protocol document might be a better place? But, going back to the core of your question, what part is confusing you? Happy to rephrase the part which is not clear or feel free to suggest what you would like to see?

The point is I've never would have gotten the idea to wait with the update for 67s. Of course the update should be signalled as soon as possible! Where did you get the impression that there is any requirement to wait? It's only the enforce that needs to be paused after an update but that even more though underlines the point that an update should always be sent as fast as possible. Adding "opportunistically" is therefore re confusing because it seems to give people the idea that this is not the expected behavior.

The protocol explicitly states in Section 7.1 that to prevent throughput advice from expiring, a network element "needs to ensure that it updates throughput advice in SCONE packets with no more than a monitoring period [67 seconds] between each update". It goes on to recommend that ideally, they update advice at least twice per monitoring period.

Section 9.2 of the protocol document also establishes the allowance for dynamic changes, stating, "Network elements MAY update more often immediately after a change in their throughput advice, to reduce the reaction time from senders".

The intent of this PR text is to bridge these requirements to account for dynamic conditions and clarify that when a dynamic condition occurs, the NE applies the change immediately. (Presumably, the NE will also reset its 67-second keep-alive window at this point). I did not mean to imply there was a scheduled 67-second timer delay before sending the signal. 

I can reword this to clarify that the network element simply relies on the arrival of the next endpoint-generated packet to send the update immediately, and also remove the word "opportunistically" since it makes the expected fast signaling sound like an exception.

Could you also clarify your point that "only the enforce needs to be paused"? Section 7.2 states that a network element should base its monitoring on the maximum value from the preceding two monitoring periods to allow applications time to adjust. By pausing enforcement, do you mean the network element should start a fresh 67-second window after the latest update is sent before enforcing the new limit, or do you mean something else in terms of how that grace period is handled?

There is no need to "bridge these requirements" because they are different requirements and completely clearly expressed in the protocol spec. The scenarios is the following:

And endpoint has to sent a scone packet at least every 67sec but best more often. Let's assume it sends one every 2s. Writing the current advice value into every scone packet every 2 second might be too much effort for an network element, so it might define it's own update interval, say every 10s,  and only write the current scone value into the next scone packet it sees after that interval expired. As long as it ends up sending the value at least once every 67s, this is sufficient to work wrongly because the signal is always valid for 67s even if a scone packet with a high values is received in-between. And yes, if the values changes it is recommended to not wait for 10s and just update the next scone packet that comes by.

However, this sufficient described in the scone protocol spec and there is no need to re-hash it in this document. If there anything unclear or even missing in the protocol spec, we should clarify it there!

> Could you also clarify your point that "only the enforce needs to be paused"? Section 7.2 states that a network element should base its monitoring on the maximum value from the preceding two monitoring periods to allow applications time to adjust. By pausing enforcement, do you mean the network element should start a fresh 67-second window after the latest update is sent before enforcing the new limit, or do you mean something else in terms of how that grace period is handled?

What I meant is covered by these "two monitoring periods": you need one period to be sure that the signal is conveyed and then you start you first actual monitoring period but you can start enforcement only at the end of that monitoring period.

> There is no need to "bridge these requirements" because they are different requirements and completely clearly expressed in the protocol spec

I agree that the core mechanics are clearly expressed in the protocol spec and  to not rehash them. However, as discussed during IETF 125, the audience for the AppMan document is network operators, and its purpose is to serve as a deployment guide. While the protocol spec defines the boundaries, operators need explicit guidance on how to configure their Network Elements within those boundaries.

>  so it might define it's own update interval, say every 10s, and only write the current scone value into the next scone packet it sees after that interval expired. As long as it ends up sending the value at least once every 67s, this is sufficient to work wrongly because the signal is always valid for 67s even if a scone packet with a high values is received in-between. And yes, if the values changes it is recommended to not wait for 10s and just update the next scone packet that comes by.

Your example of configuring a 10-second (or whatever value a network operator deems suitable) update interval to optimize CPU load, and your exact breakdown of how to configure traffic policers for the two-period enforcement delay, are perfect examples of operational deployment strategies that belong in this document.

I am open to update and rewrite the section to remove any rehashing of the protocol rules. Instead, the text can strictly focus on operator configuration, using your examples for update intervals and enforcement tuning.
Do we still need this section?

@mirjak the reason I would say to consider keeping Dynamic Updates is because it is like a "Trigger" for actioning on immediate reactions. 

It tells the operator what to do when a sudden network event happens (like a handover or hitting a data cap). It advises them to immediately update the very next available packet, rather than waiting for the normal retransmission interval we discussed in the Retransmission section.

As far as the text is concerned, I have whittled it down to something like:

"Target throughput advice can change dynamically due to access network handovers or changes in subscriber policy (e.g., reaching data thresholds). When such a change occurs, the network element can immediately update the next available traversing SCONE packet with the new throughput limit rather than waiting for its normal update interval, thereby minimizing the application's reaction time to the new network state."

I'm also open to re-evaluate once we have the full document. I am beginning to lose track of what we have and where. I do suspect, we prolly are saying the same thing at two different places.

Text:
**Presence of SCONE Network Elements on the Data Path**

In topologies where multiple SCONE-capable network elements exist on the same data path (for example, a mobile UPF and a downstream enterprise Wi-Fi gateway), operators can deploy and manage these elements completely independently. Operators do not need to implement control-plane coordination or synchronization between different network elements to negotiate rate limits. 

Because the core SCONE protocol inherently resolves multiple signals by preserving the most restrictive throughput advice along the path, each network element can simply apply its own local policy without requiring awareness of the presence, capabilities, or configuration of other network elements.

The sentence feels strange as it talks about congestion control mechanisms, where still packet loss and delay are the primary signals, and where ECN and L4S are additional signals. So maybe reformulate this sentence to: 

SCONE throughput advice is not a substitute for congestion control
mechanisms in transport protocols, utilizing congestion feedback and signals such as acknowledgements, Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), and Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S) (see Section 3.1 of {{I-D.ietf-scone-protocol}}).

I think it would be more important to talk about application use cases here. The network doesn't really have any sue cases because it doesn't really know what the traffic is; it only knows that the traffic is scone-enabled or not and can either support scone or not. Of course there is the question on what values to set the throughput advise to but I wouldn't call that a use case; it's more depend on what kind of information you have available in the network element and as such the advise might be static or adapted more dynamically.
Why is that out of scope? I don't think we need to discuss those policies but that a topic which I think would be explicitly in scope for a manageability document.
However, note that I don't think it should be covered in this section. There is already another section covering this roughly currently named "Dynamic updates".
I don't understand what you mean by "harmonising"? Don't you say above rightfully that these signal are independent?

```suggestion
(see Section 3.1 of {{I-D.ietf-scone-protocol}}).
In other words, in the best case the throughput advice is below the congestion limit
and when the application adheres to the advice, congestion control would be
application-limited and not go into action. However, in cases of e.g. high load,
congestion control would limit the throughput below the provided advice
as the scone advice is only an upper limit. As such congestion control or
a similar mechanism to react to congestion, e.g. a circuit breaker,
is always needed, in addition to SCONE.
```

This is an excellent point and definitely needs the clarification. I have incorporated your suggested reformulation into the text to reflect how transport protocols utilize both primary feedback (acknowledgments) and additional explicit signals (ECN/L4S). Thank you for catching this.

You make a very fair point. Since this is a Manageability document, explicitly declaring methods or policy determination "out of scope" may create unnecessary confusion. Also, as you correctly noted, we already provide the necessary context for what drives these policies (such as access network changes or subscriber limits) in the "Dynamic Updates" section, so we don't need to rehash it here. I can simply remove the whole "out-of-scope" sentence from the congestion control section so it remains tightly focused on L4S and ECN interworking.

You are completely right. The network is fundamentally unaware of the specific application traffic and doesn't have use cases per se. It simply provides static or dynamically adapted advice based on its policies. I will  remove the phrase "use case" when referring to the network. I can add a clarification to this section explicitly stating that the network provides the policy-driven advice (whether static or dynamic), while it is up to the applications (such as ABR video or bulk transfers) to apply that advice to their specific use cases. 
So, the first paragraph (adding Magnus' suggestion and also removing the out of scope and use case):

"SCONE throughput advice is not a substitute for congestion control mechanisms in transport protocols utilizing congestion feedback and signals such as acknowledgments, Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), and Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S). Rather, they are complementary. Congestion signals provide real-time information on loss, delay, and transient congestion for a network path, typically operating on the time scale of a round-trip time (RTT). In contrast, SCONE throughput advice operates over a much longer period. Because the network element is generally unaware of the specific application traffic, it simply provides static or dynamically adapted advice based on available policy information. Operators can use SCONE to communicate these maximum allowable bit-rates driven by video optimization, subscriber data, or load management policies, independent of instantaneous link congestion. It is then up to the applications, such as adaptive bitrate video clients or bulk transfer tasks, to utilize this advice according to their specific use cases."

Thank you for the excellent suggested text! I have accepted your phrasing directly here in the PR to incorporate it into the draft.

Just a quick note: because we are making a few additional updates to this section (to address Magnus's feedback on acknowledgments and your earlier comments regarding L4S co-deployment and network use cases), I will be submitting a broader revised text for this section a bit later. That upcoming revision will fully integrate and preserve this phrasing you've provided. Thanks again for the help!

Based on  the discussions during IETF126, here is the suggested text for Masque with SCONE (General Tunneling Considerations)

In a scenario when the traffic flows are tunneled with MASQUE (QUIC-on-QUIC tunneling), and if the endpoints receive SCONE advice for the inner QUIC flow and for the outer QUIC-flow, the endpoints need to handle the SCONE advice on the flow on which it is received.`

If this is agreeable, we will create a new PR for this change and close this PR.

```suggestion
the MASQUE client has to decide how to share the capacity among all tunneled connections.
```

General comment here rather than a specific one: don't use the word "manage" for what a network element does with SCONE.  It's a request (albeit with teeth) to endpoints.  Saying "manage" implies a degree of control that doesn't exist.
Not as bad as "manage", but "upper bound on capacity" implies more certainty than exists in practice.

```suggestion
might receive two different throughput advice values. The client should take the minimum of the throughput values.
```

From the perspective of the endpoint, the advice doesn't apply to the same thing at all, so this is not a good framing.

You should instead say that one applies to the tunnel (as above) and the other applies to the tunneled flow.  It should be obvious, of course, that the capacity of the tunnel will constrain how much the tunneled flow can use, so it makes sense to reduce the value associated with the tunneled flow to consider any lower rate received for advice on the tunnel.  Your framing could be read as applying in the opposite direction.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
@billwuqin 
 Yes, as it stands, Issue #21  is presently addressed within the "Determining Throughput Constraints" subsection (under the new Operational Considerations section in PR #39).  That subsection gives examples of how operators derive advice subscriber/data-plan policies (PCF -->SMF --> UPF in 5G, PCRF -->P-GW in 4G and also BNG and Wi-Fi), application-specific policies, dynamic conditions such as RAT handovers, and capacity/load management. These are just a handful of illustrative examples and definitely not an exhaustive list. 

We would greatly appreciate if chairs and WG can review #39  section as a whole and weigh in on the subject of Operational Considerations (stays or comes out). And if it comes out, any subsections can stay (or not)? Until then, I'd suggest Issue #21 to remain open.

Lastly, I incorrectly tagged issue #21 to PR #34, but PR #34  is really the Interworking with Other Congestion Management Mechanisms rework (ECN/L4S etc). PR #34 addresses Issues #12, #15, #16, and #23). It doesn't contain the "how throughput constraints are determined" material, so that reference was misleading.

comments.body: Closing this because the content has been split into two focused PRs on current main. PR #42 adds the standalone Determining Throughput Constraints section (Issue #21), and PR #43 adds a short Operational Considerations section and expands the title to "Applicability, Manageability and Operational Considerations" (Issue #38). The text in this PR had drifted from main, so it was redone fresh in those PRs rather than reusing the stale version.
Can we maybe just have the subsection and not this intro text as the whole document is basically on operational considerations?

(We might want some language here pointing out that the whole doc is basically operational considerations though)
I'm fine either way so please decide which way we want to go and then I will use my scalpel to work through the section.

As a contributor to SCONE (not as AD), I liked the idea of a short operational considerations section that says something like: SCONE requires configuration in servers and clients; network devices that forward QUIC packets ought to also forward packets including SCONE. Specific network devices can implement and configure the SCONE Network Element function. These aspects are discussed in /this document/. ... And I heard a suggestion that the WG added a similar statement to the protocol spec that said about the same but pointed to the /applicability and manageability document/.  It's one approach that might be clear?

@gorryfair, here is what we currently have:

**4. Operational Considerations**
Although the core SCONE protocol specifies how throughput advice is communicated to endpoints, deploying SCONE requires network operators to integrate this signaling into their existing operational, policy, and management frameworks. To implement a complete and effective solution, operators must address several operational lifecycle phases, including **policy configuration, fault detection, and performance monitoring**.

This section outlines the practical operational considerations and manageability requirements for deploying SCONE within an operator network, ensuring that SCONE Network Elements can reliably determine, deliver, and monitor throughput advice while addressing real-world network challenges.

And then the subsections are proposed (but not fully developed except for 4.1. Determining Throughput Constraints).

I see there are questions, one if section on the need for a section (sec 4) and if agreeable, what suitable subsections to address. At this points, we are awaiting further decision on the present introductory text in 4 and the 4.1 subsection (which starts to address "policy configuration" part in 4.1). Some of the feedback and discussions at the last interim was that going into operator policy may be challenging as this will vary by operator and presumably this is not exhaustive. 

I would like to get some clarity on this whole section so we can take action accordingly. 

For completeness here, I am adding the text as included in the PR above for section 4.1 

**4.1. Determining Throughput Constraints**
The specific algorithms used to calculate throughput advice are highly dependent on an operator's internal business logic and network architecture. In practice, however, these constraints are generally determined by mapping established network policies and real-time conditions into SCONE signals. To implement a complete solution, operators typically derive their throughput advice from one or more of the following operational inputs: 

**Subscriber Policies and Data Plans:** Rate limits may be triggered when a subscriber reaches specific data plan thresholds or usage caps. For example, in a 5G architecture, the User Plane Function (UPF) acting as the SCONE network element receives Quality of Service (QoS) and charging policy rules from the Policy Control Function (PCF) via the Session Management Function (SMF). Similarly, in a 4G network, the Packet Data Network Gateway (P-GW) applies policies received from the Policy and Charging Rules Function (PCRF). Beyond mobile networks, this applies equally to wireline broadband networks enforcing policies at a Broadband Network Gateway (BNG), or enterprise Wi-Fi networks where rate limits are enforced at an Access Point (AP) or wireless LAN controller.

**Application-Specific Policies:** Operators may configure specific maximum bit-rates allowed for certain types of traffic based on the user's subscription tier or device type. This includes video optimization policies for adaptive bitrate video, as well as traffic shaping policies applied to low-priority bulk downloads (such as background software updates).

**Dynamic Network Conditions:** Constraints can be updated dynamically due to changes in the access network type, such as Radio Access Technology (RAT) handovers when a user moves between 5G and 4G coverage areas.
Capacity and Load Management: During periods of unusually high usage, persistent overuse, or temporary equipment faults, the network element might signal a temporarily reduced throughput advice to manage shared capacity and guide application network usage.

By utilizing these policy rules and network conditions, operators establish the inputs necessary for the SCONE network element to dynamically determine and apply the appropriate throughput advice for a given flow.

pulls.title: Issue #48, Add diagnosis guidance for throughput advice not followed
pulls.author: smishra1200
pulls.body:
Issue #48,   Add a paragraph at the end of the Monitoring and Logging section to help operators distinguish between a delivery failure and application non-compliance when throughput advice does not appear to be followed. References Section 3.5 and Section 7.2 of I-D.ietf-scone-protocol for the advisory signal behavior and monitoring guidance respectively.

Added Text:
When throughput advice does not appear to be followed, it is useful to determine whether the advice reached the application at all, or whether the application received it but did not act on it. Operators can narrow the diagnosis by correlating the rate of SCONE advisories issued at the network element against the observed per-flow throughput over the following two monitoring periods. If the network element successfully updates traversing SCONE packets during that window but the flow's throughput does not change, it indicates either that the packets were dropped downstream before reaching the application, or that the application received the advice but did not act upon it, as SCONE is an advisory signal per Section 3.5 of I-D.ietf-scone-protocol. Conversely, if the network element stops observing traversing SCONE packets arriving from the sender, this suggests either an upstream delivery failure or the endpoint is no longer sending SCONE packets on that flow. Recording both the timestamps of issued advisories and the subsequent per-flow throughput measurements in the logging infrastructure makes this correlation possible, aligning with the monitoring guidance in Section 7.2 of
I-D.ietf-scone-protocol.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
**On the scope of this change generally**

A rewrite spanning three sections at once makes it harder to catch what shifts along the way. Two concrete examples from this diff: the sentence "network element might prioritize updating updating the next traversing SCONE packet" has a duplicated word, and the cross reference to Processing Complexity is removed. That sentence was the only link in the document connecting the reliability and cadence guidance to the CPU overhead tradeoff described in Processing Complexity. Without it, Processing Complexity is now an orphaned section, not pointed to from anywhere else in the document, and a reader following the reliability guidance has no way to find the related CPU cost consideration. Neither issue is large on its own, but they show what happens when several sections move at once. The original text also had a matched pair of cases, one sentence each for a network enforcing dynamic policies and a network enforcing fixed, subscription based policies. Only the fixed policy sentence remains here. The dynamic policy case now appears separately under Dynamic Updates, reframed around a specific trigger event, without a sentence connecting the two back together.

Given this, and that PR #63 and issue #64 are touching related scope at the same time, I would rather work through one section at a time here before taking on the larger structural change.

**On "Reliability and Mitigating Packet Loss"**

On the mitigation point specifically, deciding an update cadence is itself the active step, not passive background. The text already says operators "may choose to process and update SCONE packets more frequently to better mitigate packet losses." That is a strategy operators can choose to adopt, not something happening to them. So I would say operators do have to actively decide on a cadence strategy, and that decision is the mitigation.

On the "background information" point, agreed that the ceiling set by the endpoint isn't guidance itself. That is a fact for the operator to understand. But the network element's own cadence decision, including the choice to mitigate loss by updating more often, is guidance, not background. I would keep that distinction visible by keeping Reliability and Frequency of Updates as separate sections rather than folding both into one.

**On "Frequency of Updates"**

Same reasoning applies here. This section states the fact that packet cadence is decided by the application, which I agree is background the operator needs in order to follow the guidance, not guidance on its own. But that is exactly why I would keep Frequency of Updates separate from Reliability. It lets the reader clearly see which parts are background (what the endpoint controls) and which parts are guidance (what the network element should do about it). Combining them risks blurring that line rather than making it clearer.

**On "Dynamic Updates"**

Also prefer keeping Dynamic Updates separate from the other two, for the same reason. This section describes a specific case, when a subscriber reaches a data threshold or a network policy changes, and gives guidance for what the network element should do when it happens. One addition either way. The merged text drops the network policy change trigger from the original. "Target throughput advice can change dynamically while a flow is active, for example when a subscriber reaches a data threshold or a network policy changes." Worth keeping both examples regardless of how this section ends up organized.

**On the redundancy concern generally**

If the goal is fewer cross references rather than fewer sections, I would rather drop the pointer sentence linking Reliability to Frequency of Updates and Processing Complexity, than merge Reliability, Frequency of Updates, and Dynamic Updates into one section. Happy to make that smaller edit if it addresses the concern.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
**On dropping "Applicability" generally**

Looking through this document's sections, none of them do applicability style work, deciding when or whether to use SCONE, which deployment scenarios fit. All of them are manageability guidance for after SCONE is deployed. The one place the document discusses different deployment contexts, RAN versus wireline or Wi-Fi, ABR versus bulk transfer, already lives in the Introduction, not under the Applicability heading. So the content does not depend on the word being there. Agree with removing it.

**On the scope and risk of this rewrite**

Taking PR #62 and this PR together: title, abstract, the top level section heading, three merged sections, a rewritten congestion interworking section, and document terminology are all changing in the same sitting, alongside issue #64 and today's revision to PR #37. That is a large portion of the document moving at once, going into -03. Before going further, it would help to agree on what problem this solves that individual fixes would not, given each of the issues raised, applicability wording, redundancy, terminology, has a narrower fix on its own. Would rather work through this incrementally, one section at a time, than treat the size of the diff as settling the question of scope.

**On "Real-time congestion feedback mechanisms remain outside the SCONE domain"**

Original said "remain fully operational and function completely outside the SCONE domain." Agree with the change.

**On "advisory maximum sustainable rate"**

Agree with the change. Consistent with `draft-ietf-scone-protocol`, which uses "maximum sustainable throughput" throughout.

**On terminology consistency (bit-rate / rate / sustainable rate)**

This PR changes "bit-rate" to "rate" in some places, Conformance Monitoring, the relocated intro paragraph, and to "sustainable rate" in the abstract, while "bit-rate" remains elsewhere, Determining Throughput Constraints, Processing Complexity, the keyword list. The document now has three terms for the same concept. Since `draft-ietf-scone-protocol` itself uses "throughput" throughout, for example "throughput advice," "maximum sustainable throughput," would rather this document converge on "throughput" everywhere instead of introducing "rate" as a fourth variant. Happy to do a pass to make this consistent once the wording elsewhere settles.

**On "Presence of SCONE Network Elements On the Data Path"**

This PR drops the closing sentence, "This lets operators deploy and manage SCONE network elements independently, without building integration between them." That sentence stated the operator benefit of the independence just described. Everything before it is mechanism, this was the one line translating it into why it matters to an operator. Would like to keep it.

**On "telecommunications service provider networks" to "communication networks"**

What is the reasoning for this change? The rest of the document is written from a service provider perspective, for example subscriber data plans and PCF to SMF signaling in Determining Throughput Constraints, RAN handovers and mobility events in Change of Network Element During an Active Flow, and the Broadband Network Gateway example for wireline and Wi-Fi deployments earlier in the intro. If the intended scope is now broader than telecommunications service provider networks, these examples would need to either generalize or stay as illustrations within a broader scope. Would like to understand the intent before this changes.

**On the section heading "Manageability Considerations"**

Agree that dropping "Applicability" here doesn't lose anything, per the point above. On Considerations versus Guidance: prefer Considerations alone. The document is Informational, "Considerations" matches the convention used elsewhere in this document, Security Considerations, IANA Considerations, and Considerations and Guidance together would be redundant.

Separately, this also drops "Operational" from the original heading, "Applicability, Manageability and Operational Considerations." The section still covers Network Element Overload Handling, Conformance Monitoring, and Monitoring and Logging, and operational guidance was specifically added to this document as part of the opsdir review. So "Operational" still describes real content here, and would keep it.

**Other places to remove "applicability":** the frontmatter title, docname, and keyword list still say "applicability." Since the intent is to remove it throughout, these would need the same pass.

As stated in {{Section 3.1 of I-D.ietf-scone-protocol}}, SCONE
throughput advice is not a substitute for congestion control, which
reacts to congestion signals such as packet loss, delay, and
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) {{RFC3168}}. Low Latency, Low
Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S) {{RFC9330}} also relies on ECN
for signaling. Rather, SCONE and congestion control are
complementary.

Congestion control applies a throughput limit different from the
signaled SCONE advice. Congestion control manages the immediate
dynamics of the bottleneck link, while SCONE informs the application
of the maximum bitrate allowed by network policy. Congestion signals
provide real-time information on transient congestion for a network
path, typically operating on the time scale of a round-trip time
(RTT), whereas SCONE throughput advice operates over a much longer
period.

In the best case, the throughput advice is below the congestion
limit, and when the application adheres to the advice, congestion
control would be application-limited and not go into action.
However, in cases of high load, congestion control would limit the
throughput below the provided advice, as the SCONE advice is only an
upper limit. As such, congestion control or a similar mechanism to
react to congestion, such as a circuit breaker, is always needed in
addition to SCONE.

Operators can use SCONE to communicate static or dynamically adapted
advice based on available policy information, such as subscriber
data or load management policies, independent of instantaneous link
congestion. It is then up to the applications, such as adaptive
bitrate video clients or bulk downloads, to utilize this advice
according to their specific use cases.

Network operators can deploy SCONE alongside L4S or standard ECN as
two independent network functions. SCONE advice is carried within
the QUIC payload, independent of the IP-layer ECN field, and
updating the advice does not interact with or modify ECN markings.
Real-time congestion feedback mechanisms remain outside the SCONE
domain.

In environments where both are present, network operators will
benefit from ensuring that throughput advice policies and congestion
control configurations are consistent within scoped deployments, to
avoid providing conflicting feedback to applications.

Alternative to #62, submitted for comparison, not intended to merge
until we have compared it against #62 and settled on a direction. See
the heads-up comment on #62 for context.

into one section, retitled "Reliability of Throughput Advice Delivery"
(drops "Mitigating Packet Loss" from the title, agreeing with @mirjak ). 

Frequency of Updates carried no independent operator guidance on its own, 
so its one fact (cadence is endpoint-controlled) becomes the opening context 
for why the network element needs its own update interval, rather than a
separate section restating it.

Keeps Dynamic Updates as its own section, since the trigger-response
guidance there (act promptly on a threshold or policy change) is
distinct in kind from the steady-state cadence guidance above it.
Restores a second trigger example, a network-wide policy taking effect
while a flow is already active, alongside the data-threshold example.

No change to any other section.

pulls.author: smishra1200
pulls.body:
Addresses Issue #94.

Expands the Conformance Measurement section with the fuller explanation of why the monitoring window spans two monitoring periods, following up on Martin Thomson's explanation on the list responding to Gorry Fairhurst's AD review via PR #159. Covers the two delay sources behind the window (packet-gap cadence as the dominant one, packet loss as the second), an example of when a network element might justify a shorter window, and the tradeoff the protocol itself flags for doing so.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body: Note on sequencing: this merged while resolving a stale-citation CI failure that required catching the branch up with main, ahead of your confirmation on the review comments above. Happy to open a follow-up PR if either of you wants changes.

I wonder if the wording can be a bit more prescriptive here?
Scone advice imply to some degree that 67 second monitoring periods are in effect. And as pointed out, if operators choose shorter cycles they risk misclassifying flows, defeating the purpose of the protocol. 
It's good to mention the risks, but I'd like to see some slightly stronger advice against shorter windows.

This paragraph motivates why the monitoring period after an update is two times 67, however, the first part of the delay is covered by the maximum time until the next scone packet is received; this is actually know to the network element. The important part is to then wait another 67 in case the first packet was lost (neglecting potential other small delays). Only this is the part that needs motivation/explanation here. Then, simply waiting 2 periods is just a simplification to keep a fixed mentoring period, rather than restarting the monitoring after the signal was actually send. This is still much better explain in the protocol spec draft and I don't we should try to duplicate text here, rather then pointing to the protocol spec. I would preference to cut this paragraph down to only the first sentence.

There are two point mixed up here. a) how long do I have to wait until I can expect the new advice to be active and b) how long do I have to then monitor until I can conclude that a flow (for whatever reason is not complaint). The answer to point b is always at least 67s. So the only thing you could shorten is to not wait for 2 times 67s. Here I would say it is save to e.g. implement that if you have send at least two scone updated, you re-start the monitoring period of 67s and then after that 67s you can make a decision. If you don't want to track sending up scone updates that closely, just waiting for 2 periods is on the safe side and simpler.

comments.author: zaheduzzaman
comments.body:
I think, we should try to cover the tunnel cases as generic as possible and then if we like we treat masque as an special case and be clear on why that is special. We also should be mentioning that scone endpoints may not be aware of tunnelling happed on the path.

I see there are two cases when we have tunnels

- Security tunnels : which hides SCONE packets completely from the SCONE NE, from the point tunneling is applied, unless the tunneling endpoint is SCONE aware. In this case, current text could be modified to describe the case and use masque as an example.
- Encapsulation tunnel : in this case the SCONE NE might be able to see the SCONE packets if they are aware of the encapsulation semantics. Currently we don't cover this case.

I would suggest that we structure this section to cover this two cases.

comments.author: smishra1200
comments.body:
Thanks @zaheduzzaman, @mirjak and @gorryfair. Here is a proposed rewrite of Section 3.13 that tries to address all your comments:

```text
## Tunnels and Encapsulation

Tunnels and other encapsulation are common in networks, for example for VPNs or
traffic engineering. A SCONE-capable network element can only provide throughput
advice to a flow if it can identify that flow's SCONE packets.

If a tunnel encrypts the traffic it carries, network elements between the tunnel
endpoints cannot see the inner SCONE packets, and the inner flow receives no
throughput advice from them. A tunnel endpoint that implements the SCONE network
element function can still provide throughput advice to the inner flow. If the
encapsulation is not encrypted, only a network element configured to parse the
encapsulation headers can identify the inner SCONE packets. In either case,
receiving no throughput advice does not mean that no limits apply on the path
({{Section 5.4 of SCONE}}).

SCONE is negotiated by QUIC endpoints, so a tunnel can use SCONE only if the
tunnel is itself a QUIC connection, such as one using MASQUE
{{?I-D.schinazi-masque-proxy}}. QUIC flows that the tunnel carries can also use
SCONE. When such a tunnel carries one SCONE-capable flow, a SCONE-capable network
element on the path of the tunnel can provide throughput advice only to the
tunnel, which is the outermost flow ({{Section 3.3 of SCONE}}).
As for any tunnel, a tunnel endpoint can provide throughput advice to the inner
flows. This document does not specify how it takes the tunnel's throughput advice
into account.

When a tunnel carries multiple flows, throughput advice on the tunnel applies to
the tunnel as a whole. Throughput advice that a tunnel endpoint provides to an
inner flow applies to that flow only. Which inner flows receive throughput advice
is a matter of local policy at the tunnel endpoint. If a tunnel endpoint is also
the application endpoint, a QUIC flow tunneled in QUIC might therefore have
multiple, independent pieces of throughput advice.

If only some of the traffic in the tunnel follows throughput advice, for example
because the tunnel also carries traffic that does not use SCONE, the tunnel's
throughput can exceed the throughput advice provided for the tunnel
({{Section 3.5 of SCONE}}).

SCONE on a QUIC-based tunnel can also enable throughput advice for tunneled non-QUIC
traffic, but only if there is an interface or mechanism at the tunnel endpoint
that provides the throughput advice to the application.
```

@mirjak, happy to work from your text instead if you prefer.
